t: I was building an AI company between burger orders and honestly I miss it. I keep looking at this photo and it's kinda crazy. Simply Smashed was on its second location. Peruvian Street Kitchen was on its first. And somewhere in between both of those I decided this was also where I'd start building an AI content company on Replit. I had my laptop wedged into whatever corner I could find, squinting at code I barely understood while delivery drivers walked in and out. I'd be mid-prompt and someone would shout that orders were backing up so I'd get stuck in packing rice boxes and saucing them up. Then come back to my laptop trying to remember what I was even building. If the rush got too much the laptop just got closed and that was that. I'd been training writers at a ghostwriting agency and I could see so clearly that the whole industry was about to flip. Like I could literally feel it. And I had this thing in my head going if I don't start building this right now, from this kitchen, on this dying laptop, someone else is going to do it and I'll be watching from behind a fryer. It wasn't a plan btw. I didn't sit down and map anything out. Two food brands running, a kitchen that's too small for any of this, and my brain just going "yeah but what if we also built a tech company from here." I physically couldn't not do it. That was a couple of months ago. Draper is now past ramen profitable and growing every month. Peruvian Street Kitchen is opening its second physical location soon iA. Everything is better now. Better setup, better tools, actual laptops that work. But I keep coming back to this photo because something about building from that kitchen felt different and I can't fully explain why. P.S: I'm a firm believer that being in the trenches means delaying your trim, you have to earn it as a reward.

I've left Simply Smashed. After 2 years of building the highest rated burger joint in London, I'm stepping back. My brother's taking over day-to-day. I'm building something new. It's strange to write that. This was never supposed to be my thing. My dad has been in the food industry for over 35 years. Started in a tiny French seaside town called Dieppe where it felt like we were the only asian family around, been doing this since before I was born. The restaurant was always his world. Then my parents got on a flight to Bangladesh and lockdown got announced mid-air. Me and my brother suddenly had a restaurant with no customers, staff who needed paying, and rent that didn't care about pandemics. We ran the Help Our Heroes campaign, delivered thousands of pizza slices to hospitals across London, kept the lights on for months. When we started thinking about selling, a buyer came in and made my dad feel like a fool. Said we were "bleeding out." Made a lowball offer so insulting my dad slammed the table and walked out. They just smirked and lit cigarettes outside. That led to a chain of events which led up to starting Simply Smashed. We launched three concepts at once. Simply Smashed just happened to be the one that took off. A £100 grill. Tables pushed away. The front space rented to a flower shop so people walked through flowers to pick up their burgers. We had no money to do it properly so we just told people what we were building and let them watch us figure it out. Today we're rated 4.9 stars. The highest rated burger joint in London. Looking back now it's hard to separate Simply Smashed from my family. My dad showing up every single time we needed him. My brother building operations that actually worked. My sister-in-law who created half the recipes we still serve today. We got review bombed for stocking Salaam Cola and the community showed up for us. Grateful for all of it. This was always a family thing. It still is. My brother has been with us from early and I trust him completely to take Simply Smashed and Peruvian Street Kitchen forward. I'm not disappearing - I'll still be around for strategic oversight. But the day-to-day is his now. Excited to see where he takes them both. I'm building something new. Can't say much yet but if you followed the Simply Smashed journey, you know the playbook. More soon iA.

I abandoned my restaurant mid-service to bike across London while my kitchen was on fire. "Just sell chicken burgers until I get back," I told my team. Then I ran out the door. The cables had just burst into flames. Smoke filling the kitchen. My dad took one look at the melting electrical panel and rattled off exactly what I needed from Screwfix. So there I was - racing through 20 London lanes on a Santander bike, while customers wondered why beef burgers suddenly went "out of stock." They never knew their food was delayed because the owner literally abandoned them. 2 hours later, we were back online. That was Simply Smashed, 14 months ago. Last month, I found myself in another kitchen. Different location. New menu. Same game. But this time, when I flipped the switches, checked the electrical loads, and fired up the grills - no panic. No surprises. Just muscle memory from 14 months of controlled chaos. PSK - Peruvian Street Kitchen - went from idea to serving customers in 2 weeks. Not because we rushed. Because we already knew every shortcut. Every supplier's direct line. Every permit loophole. Every mistake to avoid. The same hands that once scrambled to fix burning cables now move with precision. Set up stations. Test recipes. Train staff. Like we've done this dance a hundred times. Because we have. The early reviews are proving what experience tastes like: "Addictive" "Can't stop thinking about it" "When can I order again?" Every crisis at Simply Smashed was tuition for PSK. Every fire we put out taught us how to build something fireproof. This Sunday, November 2nd, PSK takes over Simply Smashed Stepney for one day only. The kitchen that caught fire 14 months ago now houses something built from those ashes. And we're still here, cooking.

Someone just called our chicken "crack" and we haven't even launched yet. I can't lie - that made my entire week. 14 days ago, PSK didn't exist. Now people are reordering daily during testing. "Puts Shah's to shame" "11 out of 10" People reordering the next day. From test batches. In foil containers. Before we've even dialed everything in. This is what 2 years of Simply Smashed taught us: Everything compounds. The suppliers that took months to find? One phone call for PSK. The operations we stressed over? Second nature now. We went from empty kitchen to serving testers in 14 days. Simply Smashed: 3 months to get our first "addictive" review PSK: Day 14 The difference isn't talent. It's compound learning. My WhatsApp is going crazy. Early testers sending photos. Friends asking when we open. And we haven't even launched properly. Still tweaking the green sauce. Still perfecting spice levels. Still obsessing over details only we notice. Because making food people love? That's the whole point. That's what keeps me up marinating chicken at 2am. That's why these early reviews mean everything. PSK launches next week. Starting small. Limited quantities. Want to make sure every box is right. The most addictive chicken and rice box in London? Based on these early reactions, we might actually pull it off. Can't wait for you to try it.

A customer just ordered from us 3 days straight. During testing. When we weren't even open. I'm typing this with a bandaged finger and burnt hands. Yesterday my brother Sifat and I ran the entire Peruvian Street Kitchen ourselves. No staff. Just us. Invite-only testing that turned into our busiest "quiet" evening yet. Someone rated us "11 out of 10." We sold out. We weren't even supposed to be open. But here's what happened that matters more than the sales: The first batch of chicken I grilled wasn't right. Not the standard I'd been hitting at home. Too rushed. Wrong char. By batch three, I'd found the rhythm. By batch five, it was perfect. If I'd hired someone to run that grill yesterday, I'd never have known: Why quality drops during a rush Which corners get cut under pressure What muscle memory needs to develop How the kitchen flows when orders stack up I see food founders all the time who think they can outsource from day one. Hire a chef. Hire managers. Never touch the grill themselves. Then they wonder why their food tastes different six months later. Why quality slides. Why their reviews drop. You can't train someone to maintain standards you've never held yourself. You can't teach someone to handle pressure you've never felt. You can't build a food business without burning your own hands first. My brother was filling rice boxes at lightning speed. I was cutting Peruvian chicken with a bleeding finger. We moved like we did in Simply Smashed's early days - pure instinct, no waste, complete sync. This is what being in the arena means. Not watching from the sidelines with a clipboard. Not managing from a laptop. Actually burning yourself on the same grill your team will use tomorrow. Now I'm boarding a flight with bandaged fingers and the smell of charcoal in my clothes heading to work on another project. But I know exactly what our future staff will face. Exactly where they'll struggle. Exactly how to train them. Because I bled for it first. That's how you build something real.

I've been running a secret experiment on myself for 2 months. The results are concerning. Remember that Peruvian Thigh burger? The one that had people asking for the recipe in my DMs? That was just the warm-up. While you were eating it, I was back in the kitchen asking a dangerous question: what if we went all the way? Not just a burger with Peruvian flavours. But something that ruins every other chicken and rice box in London. PSK - Peruvian Street Kitchen. That green sauce that made you pause mid-bite? We perfected it. Then gave it two siblings - a red that brings proper heat, a white that balances everything. The chicken - charred crust, stupid juicy inside. The rice - actually seasoned, soaks up every drop. Together? I've watched people go quiet mid-bite. My brother and I spent months studying NYC halal carts. Those guys turn basic ingredients into 2am cravings. But London needs its own thing. Here's where it gets interesting: Two months. Same PSK box. Every single day. Still not bored. Still excited at lunch. That's not normal. So we did something unusual. We've quietly launched PSK somewhere in London. No announcement. No address. Just word of mouth. The people who've found it? They're not telling anyone where it is. Can you find it? Pepe's, Shah's, Rio's, Nando's - respectfully - your time is up. You just don't know it yet.

I almost watched my 60-year-old dad fall off a ladder yesterday. All for a sticker. He was three stories up, no harness, leaning at an angle that made my stomach drop. My brother was holding the base. I was holding my breath. "Get down," I shouted. "I do it myself," he shouted back. The Simply Smashed sticker needed to go up. But this wasn't our usual spot. This wasn't our usual anything. Two years. One kitchen. Thousands of smashed burgers. That's been our story. Until today. Last week I cut my finger deep enough to see white. Today my dad's risking his neck for vinyl adhesive. We've had offers to grow faster. Franchise inquiries. Investors. The "scale quickly" playbook. But watching him up there - applying that second sticker way better than my rushed first one - I understood something: The families that build things that last are the ones who never stop doing the hard work themselves. My sticker had bubbles. His was perfect. My hands were shaking. His were steady. Both stickers are up now. One say Simply Smashed. The other marks something new. Our regulars have no idea what's coming. More soon. (PSK fans... stay especially tuned)

The Peruvian Thigh sold out in 3 hours on Monday. Most founders would be celebrating. I'm spending my days restocking and my evenings doing something most people don't realise restaurants need to do. Restocked at 8pm yesterday. Down to 2 left today. I'm literally restocking again as I write this. While everyone's buzzing about the 9s and 10s out of 10 we're getting, I spent yesterday doing the thing I can't stop myself from doing. 4 hours on the floor. Talking to every single customer who ordered it. Not because anything's wrong - the feedback has been insane. People are losing their minds over how tender the chicken is. Sure, one or two people said it wasn't for them. That happens. But here's what nobody tells you about launching food products: The recipe is maybe 20% of the work. The other 80%? Building systems so your staff don't ruin it. This isn't home cooking. You can't just hand someone a recipe and expect magic. I'm spending the next 2 months training every cook on exact timing. Quality control checkpoints. How to handle the marinade. When the chicken is perfectly done vs. overdone. The real skill isn't making good food. It's cutting through the noise of feedback to find what actually matters. Every "this is perfect" gets weighed against every valid criticism. What are people actually saying? What do they mean? How do we take all this data and find the one thing that improves our product? Our first Simply Smashed burger? Complete disaster. Not because the recipe was bad, but because we had no systems. No training. No quality control. I'm not a chef. But I know how to learn. How to gather feedback. How to iterate. It's very easy to get lost in the "yay, we launched a burger" celebration. But that's not it. It's the obsessiveness. The continuous improvement. The gathering data. Making sure we've got the systems in place. It's not sexy work, but it has to be done. While competitors are already planning their next launch, I'm still perfecting Monday's systems. Excellence isn't just a recipe - it's a system that delivers it every single time.

There's this lunch from my Goldman days I can't get out of my head. After 16 failed attempts, I finally know why. You know that feeling when you can't get a taste out of your head? That's what happened to me with this lunch I had 5 years ago at Goldman. There was this Peruvian place near our office. Always had these mental queues outside. I'm talking senior bankers, MDs, people who expense £300 dinners without blinking - all standing in line for chicken. One day I thought let me see what all the fuss is about. That green sauce hit me like a truck. I'm not even joking. It was so addictive I understood why grown men in Savile Row suits would abandon their desks for this. The chicken? Fell apart with a fork. Juice running down my wrist. I threw away my Tesco meal deal routine that same day. Fast forward to now. We're London's highest-rated burger joint. But here's the thing - and this is what people don't get about running Simply Smashed - the bar keeps getting higher with every single product we launch. I'm never satisfied. There's this insecurity that drives me mental. This feeling that our products aren't good enough yet. So when I couldn't shake that taste memory, I knew I had to do something about it. What if we took that inspiration and made it our own? Version 1? Complete disaster. Burnt chicken, perfect sauce, everything else wrong. By Version 16, I was losing my mind. Two months of testing marinades. Custom potato buns because our brioche was overpowering the flavors. Different cooking methods to lock in every drop of moisture. Then last week everything clicked. Our green sauce - inspired by Peru but uniquely ours. Same addictive quality but adapted for this burger. When our first customer tried it, he just looked at me wide-eyed and said "This is the best burger on your menu. How did you even make this?" That feeling? When something that's been living in your head becomes real and makes someone else happy? That's why I do this. The Peruvian Thigh launches today. Some obsessions are worth chasing. The best ones change everything when you finally catch them.
